newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan won't cut Canada grain import despite delays.
newsitem.headline: Japan won't cut Canada grain import despite delays.

text.p: The Canadian agriculture minister's visit to Japan this week to promote exports has been overshadowed by delayed grain shipments, but Japan's Food Agency said on Friday it would not cut imports as a result.
Japan is one of the largest importers of Canadian grains.
Heavy snow, extreme cold, and equipment failure have led to delays in rail shipments to Pacific ports from grain-growing regions in Canada since early January.

Yuki Takagi, the director general of Japan's Food Agency, the country's sole importer of wheat, barley and rice, said Canada was taking all possible measures to deal with the problem. "We're still confident of Canada's stable grain supply capacity, and have no plan to shift to other countries."
However, another Food Agency official said that some wheat-flour makers had been forced to shift to U.S. crops, particularly Dark Northern Spring wheat, which is mainly used for making bread.
The Food Agency had also rearranged its unloading operation of Canadian wheat to maintain sufficient supplies for all wheat-flour makers across the country, the official said.
After meeting Takagi on Thursday, Canada's Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale, told Reuters: "We described in detail what exactly we're doing to overcome the delayed shipments.
"The worst is behind us this season, and we're now meeting our target and will continue to do so for the balance of this crop year.
"For the long term, we're taking steps to make sure this kind of difficulty does not keep happening. Japanese customers are concerned, but Canada is equally concerned."
Goodale's delegation included business executives and government officials.
The Canadian Wheat Board faces more than C$15 million in demurrage charges and has acknowledged deferring sales.

Canadian Wheat Board (CWB) chief commissioner Lorne Hehn said on Thursday that grain shipments to Japan would be back to normal by early April, after transportation problems in Canada caused a severe backlog of vessels at West Coast ports.
